story_lines.meet_agnes: Agnes leaves a warm pastry and welcomes you to the neighbourhood.
story_lines.pip_reflection: Pip asks for strawberry milk. In the window, the little ghost has no reflection.
story_lines.receipt_1974: Agnes notices an old receipt in the till. It is dated 1974, with Pip's order.
story_lines.hidden_photograph: Behind the old receipt is a photograph: Pip, standing in this very shop.
story_lines.pip_first_memory: Pip remembers Moonmart as a safe place, long before tonight.
story_lines.fern_arrives: Fern visits from Whisperwood. The woods have gone so quiet that even the rain sounds far away.
story_lines.lucien_arrives: Lucien asks for decaf and a detective novel. He has read every ending except the one in his own life.
story_lines.wren_arrives: Wren Hollow brings a map with one station marked in disappearing ink.
story_lines.grove_silence: Fern shows you a grove where the birds have stopped singing. A hush curls around the roots.
story_lines.grove_restored: A robin calls from the old grove. Fern smiles as if she has been holding her breath for weeks.
story_lines.lucien_old_friend: A name is written in the margin of Lucien's detective novel: Ada, in familiar handwriting.
story_lines.lucien_reunion: Lucien sends a letter to Ada with no demand in it, only a small invitation to talk.
story_lines.wren_missing_person: Wren tells you her sister boarded a train between stations and never came home.
story_lines.wren_search_started: Wren finds her family's mark on a ticket. She decides to keep looking, with your help.
story_lines.photo_changes: The face in Agnes's old shop photograph has changed again. This time, everyone saw it.
story_lines.mara_unaddressed_letter: Mara brings a letter with no address. The postmark says Bellwether, on a day nobody remembers.
story_lines.osric_arrives: A tired passenger steps in from the rain and asks whether the morning train has arrived.
story_lines.conductor_first_appears: The Conductor appears by the window and quietly says Osric's name. The passenger remembers it too.
story_lines.long_midnight_named: Agnes tells you about the Long Midnight, the night the sun did not rise and the town chose to forget.
story_lines.map_gaps: Mara lays an old town map beside today's. A street has vanished from both, though the postmarks remember it.
story_lines.forgotten_resident_returned: Osric's name returns to the ledger. He remembers his sister and the little blue house near the quay.
story_lines.conductor_promise: The Conductor promises to show you the platform when its train is ready to stop.
story_lines.platform_ticket: Wren finds her sister's mark on a ticket to a station that does not appear on any town map.
story_lines.platform_opened: A door at the edge of the platform opens. Beyond it waits a train full of quiet, patient lights.
story_lines.passenger_manifest_read: You read every passenger's name aloud. The station seems to settle around each one.
story_lines.miso_guardian_truth: Agnes finally explains: Miso has watched this doorway for longer than the shop has had a sign.
story_lines.miso_promise: Miso presses a paw against yours. The Conductor says the old guardian may choose to stay, or choose to rest.
story_lines.lighthouse_sight: Elias has seen the lighthouse beam crossing the water again, though its lamp was removed years ago.
story_lines.elias_confesses: The lighthouse log records the Long Midnight in Elias's own handwriting. He had forgotten writing it.
story_lines.lighthouse_mechanism: Wren repairs the old lens with a shard of remembered moonlight, freely given and returned by morning.
story_lines.agnes_old_oath: Agnes admits her family kept the first agreement. It asked them to leave a light on, never to give anything up.
story_lines.lighthouse_restored: The restored beacon sweeps across the sea. Lost travellers can see the way home without being pulled toward it.
story_lines.agreement_read: The original covenant is simple: keep a safe place for anyone who needs one. The doorway was never meant to own anyone.
story_lines.travellers_gather: Pip helps welcome the travellers. Some want to stay for tea; some are ready to go home.
story_lines.miso_decides: Miso chooses what comes next. Whatever the cat decides, Moonmart will still feel like home.
story_lines.boundary_stabilized: Bellwether remembers its missing neighbours. The boundary steadies around the choices each traveller made.
story_lines.final_covenant_made: Together, the town writes a new promise for the doorway. At dawn, the shop is still warm and full of people.

ordinary_lines.agnes: Agnes says the pastries are yesterday's, but they still smell wonderful.
ordinary_lines.pip: Pip waves, strawberry milk held carefully in both hands.
ordinary_lines.fern: Fern asks if the little tea plant by the window is doing well.
ordinary_lines.lucien: Lucien recommends a mystery novel. He promises the ending is only a little implausible.
ordinary_lines.wren: Wren trades a pressed flower for a story about the town.
ordinary_lines.conductor: The Conductor tips their hat. No train is due just yet.
ordinary_lines.elias: Elias says the sea has been quieter since the beacon came back on.
ordinary_lines.mara: Mara has another letter to sort, this one with a proper address.
ordinary_lines.osric: Osric remembers the way back to the harbour and stops to say hello.
ordinary_lines.miriam_underwood: Miriam warms her hands around a coffee and tells you the bus ride home was peaceful.
ordinary_lines.hollis_quince: Hollis listens to the little clock above the door and smiles when it keeps good time.
ordinary_lines.sabine_kersey: Sabine says the harbour ropes are mended for the night and asks how the shop is keeping.
ordinary_lines.anouk_harrow: Anouk wonders which seeds would be happiest in the greenhouse window next spring.
ordinary_lines.oda_lovell: Oda taps a gentle rhythm against her notebook and says the rain has found its chorus.
ordinary_lines.elowen_charter: Elowen says every sheet came clean today, even the one with blackberry jam on it.
ordinary_lines.stellan_rusk: Stellan checks his pocket watch, then decides he has time to finish his warm milk.
ordinary_lines.iona_pebble: Iona tucks a postcard safely into her bag and asks if the sea has brought any letters back.
ordinary_lines.liora_fenwick: Liora turns a paper lantern in her hands and says this one might be ready for the next gathering.
ordinary_lines.rowan_pike: Rowan says the lighthouse inventory is finally balanced, except for one pencil that keeps moving.
ordinary_lines.maribel_frost: Maribel asks whether the inn's quiet room might suit a traveller who needs a softer night.
ordinary_lines.tomas_wicks: Tomas says the thyme beside the square wall has started to smell like summer again.
ordinary_lines.juniper_hale: Juniper found a kind little note in the archive margin and promises to copy it into the public book.
ordinary_lines.beckett_shore: Beckett says the tide brought in a bright shell and carried off one of his mittens.
ordinary_lines.nella_finch: Nella checks the seam on her handkerchief and smiles at the tiny crescent in its corner.
ordinary_lines.aster_rowe: Aster says the clouds parted long enough to make the whole night's waiting worthwhile.
ordinary_lines.ordinary_tide_table_clerk: The tide-table clerk checks a freshly printed page against the harbour bell and sighs at the difference.
ordinary_lines.ordinary_lamplighter_apprentice: The lamplighter's apprentice warms their hands on the paper cup and says one lamp on Clover Lane hums when it is happy.
ordinary_lines.ordinary_sleepwalking_teacher: The schoolteacher notices chalk on their sleeve and cannot remember writing anything at all.
ordinary_lines.ordinary_lost_property_clerk: The lost-property clerk labels everything twice, once for its owner and once for whoever it used to be.
ordinary_lines.ordinary_umbrella_mender: The umbrella mender hangs a repaired umbrella by the door and says it prefers the rain to the sunshine.
ordinary_lines.ordinary_orchard_nightwatch: The orchard watchman says the trees were whispering again, and are probably sorry about the gate.

default_ordinary_line: %s thanks you and lingers beneath the warm shop lights.

agnes_first.speaker: Agnes
lines: First night on your own, is it? The shop has a way of looking after people.
Your predecessor used to say the same thing. I suppose the shelves remember.

pip_tuesday.speaker: Pip
lines: I come here every Tuesday. I think.
The strawberry milk is pink like a sunset I nearly remember.

fern_grove.speaker: Fern
lines: There used to be birds in every branch.
I can wait. The roots are old, and quiet does not always mean gone.

wren_sister.speaker: Wren
lines: She boarded at a platform I could not find again.
I kept one ticket. I did not keep her name safe enough.

conductor_names.speaker: The Conductor
lines: A name spoken kindly can be a lamp.
I have carried many. I am glad you are helping me set them down.

elias_light.speaker: Elias
lines: They told me to stop tending a light that could not be there.
I stopped telling anyone. I never stopped looking at the shore.

mara_letters.speaker: Mara
lines: Some letters arrive without an address, but the paper still remembers where it began.
I keep a drawer for the ones that need a little more time.

osric_name.speaker: Osric
lines: I remember warm bread and rain on the quay.
The Conductor said my name. I think I can carry it now.

agnes_photograph.speaker: Agnes
lines: When Pip appeared in that photograph, I wanted to find an explanation before I found a way to listen.
You let the picture be strange without making Pip prove anything. I remember that kindness.

agnes_covenant.speaker: Agnes
lines: My family kept the old agreement as if a safe light were a debt someone had to pay.
The new words feel right: leave the door open, and let each visitor choose when to go.

pip_memory.speaker: Pip
lines: I can remember the shop now. The bell, the warm bread, and someone saving me a seat.
I still lose the details sometimes, but the safe feeling comes back when I need it.

pip_travellers.speaker: Pip
lines: Some travellers asked for tea, and some asked which way home was. We helped with both.
Miso gets to choose too. I like a promise that leaves room for everybody to say what they want.

fern_silence.speaker: Fern
lines: The hush has a shape, like snow over a path. I am glad you heard it with me.
We do not have to hurry the grove. We can keep showing up and let it answer in its own time.

fern_birds.speaker: Fern
lines: The first robin sang from the old roots. I nearly answered before I remembered to breathe.
The grove was never asking us to force it awake. It needed patience, company, and room.

lucien_ada.speaker: Lucien
lines: Finding Ada's name brought back the years I spent rehearsing what I should have said.
I am trying to remember her as a person, not as an ending I can rewrite.

lucien_letter.speaker: Lucien
lines: Ada replied. We have not solved the past; we have simply agreed to have tea.
For once, the next chapter can be small and still be worth writing.

lucien_midnight_storybook_stocked.speaker: Lucien
lines: You put the Midnight Storybook on the shelf. Its final chapter seems to have been rewritten in the margins.
I will not spoil the ending. Some mysteries are nicer when the book gets to finish them in its own time.

wren_search.speaker: Wren
lines: The family mark on that ticket is hers. I have stared at it for years and never let myself hope.
I want to keep looking, but I am learning that searching together does not mean carrying it alone.

wren_platform.speaker: Wren
lines: The train is real, and so is the choice to wait until I am ready to board.
My sister is more than the moment she vanished. I will meet her as she is, if she wants that too.

conductor_promise.speaker: The Conductor
lines: I used to think keeping every name meant keeping every passenger with me.
A name is safer when it can travel freely, spoken by someone who cares.

conductor_covenant.speaker: The Conductor
lines: The town has written a promise that shelters without binding. I can finally set down the old wording.
At dawn, every route remains a choice. That is a better duty than deciding for anyone.

elias_log.speaker: Elias
lines: Seeing my own handwriting in the lighthouse log was like meeting the part of me that kept watch.
I had forgotten the night, but the record did not ask me to carry it alone anymore.

elias_beacon.speaker: Elias
lines: The restored beam reaches the harbour and the far coast. Nobody has to follow it; it only shows the way.
I can stop mistaking a light for a command. It is enough to make a safe path visible.

mara_map.speaker: Mara
lines: The missing street was still there in the postmarks. Paper can keep a place for someone while a town forgets.
We will put the names back carefully, and ask the people who return what they want remembered.

mara_return.speaker: Mara
lines: Osric's name is back in the ledger, in ink that belongs to this morning.
I used to think an archive had to be complete to be honest. Now I leave space for people to amend their own stories.

osric_home.speaker: Osric
lines: I found the blue house by the quay. My sister's garden is wild, but I know the gate.
I do not need every lost day returned before I can take the next step home.

osric_covenant.speaker: Osric
lines: I read the town's new promise twice. It leaves the door open and leaves the choice with the person standing there.
I am staying in Bellwether for now. That is my answer today, and tomorrow I get to answer again.

side_agnes_oven_dawn.speaker: Agnes
lines: My mother always put a little orange peel in the first loaf of the morning. It made the whole kitchen smell like a new day.
I thought I had forgotten the recipe. The smell brought it back, gentle as anything.

side_agnes_ledger_flour.speaker: Agnes
lines: I found my old flour notes beside the family agreement. The margins are full of small corrections from three generations.
We were better at leaving each other useful notes than saying what we meant.

side_agnes_sunrise_loaf.speaker: Agnes
lines: That first sunrise loaf is ready. I saved you the end piece, where the crust goes crisp.
A shop can keep a promise with very ordinary things: warm bread, a light in the window, a chair left open.

side_pip_window_stars.speaker: Pip
lines: I used to count the stars in the shop window. I always lost my place when someone came in.
Maybe that was the point. The stars stayed there, and so did the people.

side_pip_names_in_jars.speaker: Pip
lines: I made labels for everyone who passed through. Some names got smudged, but I kept the jars anyway.
Would you help me write the names again? We can leave room for people who have not arrived yet.

side_pip_new_night.speaker: Pip
lines: The shop sounds different now. I can hear the kettle without worrying that it means someone is lost.
I think I would like to stay for one more cup. Then we will see.

side_fern_seed_envelope.speaker: Fern
lines: I pressed a few grove seeds into paper so they would not blow away on the walk home.
Some seeds need darkness before they wake. I try not to mistake waiting for failure.

side_fern_bird_counts.speaker: Fern
lines: I have started counting the birds again. Not to prove they are safe, just to notice who comes by.
A count can be a kind of welcome if you leave space for the unexpected.

side_fern_moss_path.speaker: Fern
lines: There is a little moss path growing over the old mark in the grove. It does not hide it; it makes room around it.
That feels right. Healing can leave the history visible and still make a soft place to stand.

side_lucien_margin_note.speaker: Lucien
lines: I found a note in the margin of a book I used to lend out. It only says, “You can bring it back whenever.”
Such a small sentence. I have carried it farther than the book.

side_lucien_library_card.speaker: Lucien
lines: The library card is still tucked inside. There is no date beside the last return.
I used to think an unfinished record meant someone had failed. Now I think it can mean there is still time.

side_lucien_open_shelf.speaker: Lucien
lines: I put the book on the open shelf. Anyone can read it, and no one has to explain why they picked it up.
That is a good way for a story to live: offered, never owed.

side_wren_route_sketch.speaker: Wren
lines: I sketched a route that ends at a blank page. My sister used to say every map needs a place for what you have not found.
I used to hate that answer. I can keep it for now.

side_wren_platform_bench.speaker: Wren
lines: There is a bench on the platform with room for two. I left the space beside me empty, but not guarded.
Waiting feels different when you are allowed to rest while you do it.

side_wren_folded_map.speaker: Wren
lines: I folded the map so the blank part sits on the outside. It is not a promise that I will find her.
It is a promise that I will keep looking without letting the search take every other road from me.

side_mara_unsent_copy.speaker: Mara
lines: I keep a copy of every letter that arrives without an address. I thought it was for the records.
Perhaps it is also a way to tell the sender their words reached someone.

side_mara_blue_postmark.speaker: Mara
lines: A blue postmark turned up on the missing-street map. It does not tell us where the street went.
It tells us somebody once took the trouble to send a letter from there.

side_mara_open_mailbox.speaker: Mara
lines: I left the little mailbox by the harbour open today. People can leave a note or take one; there is no ledger for it.
Not every message needs to be traced. Some only need a safe place to land.

side_conductor_timetable_1.speaker: The Conductor
lines: I have begun writing down the ordinary times as well as the impossible ones. The kettle boils at two; the first gull calls at four.
A timetable can be a record of being here, not an order to keep moving.

side_conductor_timetable_2.speaker: The Conductor
lines: I added a stop called Rest. It has no platform number and no onward connection.
Passengers may stay as long as they need. I am learning that a good timetable can leave a little blank space.

side_conductor_timetable_3.speaker: The Conductor
lines: The page is full of small times now: tea shared, names returned, someone choosing to sleep until morning.
I will keep the timetable, but I will not ask anyone to follow it.

side_conductor_platform_lamps_1.speaker: The Conductor
lines: The platform lamps used to be lit only when a train was expected. I have left one burning for the people who are not sure.
It is a small light. It does not need to decide anyone's direction.

side_conductor_platform_lamps_2.speaker: The Conductor
lines: A traveller left a paper star beneath the lamp. Another left a seed packet, and neither asked for a receipt.
The platform is beginning to look like somewhere people can rest between journeys.

side_conductor_platform_lamps_3.speaker: The Conductor
lines: I added a bench beside the lamp. It is wide enough for a friend, or for a person who would rather sit alone.
No tickets are needed to rest here.

side_elias_lens_cloth_1.speaker: Elias
lines: The lens cloth has a little tear near one corner. I kept using it for years because it was the one I had that night.
Wren found me a new one. I think I can let the old cloth become just a cloth now.

side_elias_lens_cloth_2.speaker: Elias
lines: The new cloth leaves no streaks. I cleaned the lens slowly and watched the harbour come into focus.
For once, I looked at the boats without counting who might be missing.

side_elias_lens_cloth_3.speaker: Elias
lines: I have put the old cloth in the drawer with the logbook. It can stay there without being a warning.
Tomorrow I will polish the lantern because it needs polishing. That is reason enough.

side_elias_weather_log_1.speaker: Elias
lines: I started a weather log with no column for the Long Midnight. Just cloud, wind, and whether the sea was kind to the boats.
It feels good to write down a night without asking it to explain itself.

side_elias_weather_log_2.speaker: Elias
lines: The rain came in softly, and the beacon made a pale path across it. A fisherman waved from the far pier.
I wrote 'steady rain, safe return' and left the page at that.

side_elias_weather_log_3.speaker: Elias
lines: The log has a dozen ordinary entries now. I thought I would miss the old mystery more than I do.
Some nights are allowed to be only themselves.

side_osric_quay_garden_1.speaker: Osric
lines: My sister's garden is still waiting behind the blue gate. The thyme has grown over the stepping stones.
I thought I needed to remember every afternoon before I could go back. I can begin with this morning.

side_osric_quay_garden_2.speaker: Osric
lines: We cleared a small patch beside the gate. My sister planted mint there, though neither of us remembers why.
We decided the reason can stay lost. The mint smells lovely either way.

side_osric_quay_garden_3.speaker: Osric
lines: There is a chair in the garden now. I can sit there without trying to reconstruct every missing day.
My sister brought tea. We talked about the weather, and it was enough.

side_osric_bread_route_1.speaker: Osric
lines: I walked from the quay to Moonmart by the bakery this morning. Fresh bread has a very persuasive smell.
I used to follow that smell without knowing where I was going. I am glad my feet still remember the way.

side_osric_bread_route_2.speaker: Osric
lines: Agnes gave me a paper bag for the walk home. The crust warmed my hands through it.
I used to think a homecoming had to restore everything. This one only asked me to carry bread carefully.

side_osric_bread_route_3.speaker: Osric
lines: My sister says I can come by whenever I like. I do not have to wait for a special reason or the right memory.
I think I will take the bakery route again tomorrow.

side_agnes_night_baker_1.speaker: Agnes
lines: I have started baking a smaller batch at night. The customers who come in before dawn deserve something fresh, too.
It is easier on my hands, and there is less left over. I should have tried it years ago.

side_agnes_night_baker_2.speaker: Agnes
lines: I pinned the new schedule by the oven. Fern added a note reminding me to rest between batches.
The note is annoyingly sensible. I have decided to follow it.

side_agnes_night_baker_3.speaker: Agnes
lines: My niece came by at sunrise to learn the honey loaf. She had flour on her nose before we finished the first bowl.
The recipe is older than the shop, but it can belong to whoever wants to bake it.

side_mara_harbour_post_1.speaker: Mara
lines: I found a little postbox near the harbour steps. It has no lock, and the salt air has worn away the paint.
Someone left a folded note inside. It was only a drawing of a boat coming home.

side_mara_harbour_post_2.speaker: Mara
lines: I brought a tin of pencils to the postbox. People have left sketches, recipes, and one very detailed list of clouds.
No names are needed. The notes can be read, answered, or left in peace.

side_mara_harbour_post_3.speaker: Mara
lines: The postbox has a fresh coat of blue paint now. The net-mender says it matches the harbour on a clear night.
It is a place for messages without an address. I think that is a kind of belonging.

side_miriam_night_route_1.speaker: Miriam
lines: I keep a thermos for the last stretch, when the buses are mostly empty and the rain sounds louder than the engine.
A warm cup makes the quiet feel like company. I have started leaving an extra one for anyone who needs it.

side_miriam_night_route_2.speaker: Miriam
lines: There is a stop by the old orchard where nobody gets on anymore. I still pause there; the trees deserve a little patience.
Last night, a tired walker waved from the shelter. The route was useful in a new way.

side_miriam_night_route_3.speaker: Miriam
lines: I used to call the depot the end of the line. Now I think of it as the place where the next driver gets a fresh cup of tea.
A route can finish for one person and begin for another. That is a good thing to remember.

side_hollis_clockwork_1.speaker: Hollis
lines: The clock above my bench runs two minutes slow. I could fix it, but I have been listening to its softer beat first.
Some rooms need a rhythm that leaves a little space around the hour.

side_hollis_clockwork_2.speaker: Hollis
lines: I repaired the chime without making it louder. The neighbours can hear it, but it no longer startles the baby upstairs.
Good work should fit the lives around it, not ask everyone to fit the work.

side_hollis_clockwork_3.speaker: Hollis
lines: A child brought me a clock made from a tin lid and a paper sun. It cannot tell time, but it keeps excellent company.
I hung it beside the careful one. They both have something to teach me.

side_sabine_mended_net_1.speaker: Sabine
lines: I found a tear in the smallest net and repaired it with the old blue cord. The knots came back to my hands before the memory did.
Mending is mostly a way of saying the thing is worth keeping close.

side_sabine_mended_net_2.speaker: Sabine
lines: We made a spare net for the harbour steps. It is light enough for children to help with and strong enough for a basket of apples.
Everyone added a knot. Nobody had to sign their name.

side_sabine_mended_net_3.speaker: Sabine
lines: The spare net caught a drifting parcel before the tide carried it away. It was only a loaf and a note, but somebody was glad to get both back.
I like when useful things get to be ordinary again.

side_anouk_seed_exchange_1.speaker: Anouk
lines: The greenhouse seedlings leaned toward the door this morning. I moved the pots so they could have the pale window light instead.
Care sometimes means changing the room before asking anything of the growing thing.

side_anouk_seed_exchange_2.speaker: Anouk
lines: I set out a seed tin with blank labels. People can take a packet, leave one, or simply read the names.
A garden is easier to join when nobody has to know everything first.

side_anouk_seed_exchange_3.speaker: Anouk
lines: The empty tins are filling with notes about where each plant likes to grow. Someone wrote, 'near a friend,' beside the nasturtiums.
I think that is good advice for seedlings and people.

side_oda_rain_song_1.speaker: Oda
lines: I wrote down the rain's rhythm, then noticed I had left no rests between the notes.
The quiet between sounds is part of the song. I am trying to let it stay.

side_oda_rain_song_2.speaker: Oda
lines: We tried the new tune at the chapel with only three voices. Nobody had to sing the high part; the melody held together anyway.
It sounded more like us than a perfect performance ever could.

side_oda_rain_song_3.speaker: Oda
lines: The choir wants to keep the tune for ordinary evenings, not just the festival. We will sing it softly enough for people to join or listen.
A song can offer a seat without calling anyone onto the stage.

side_elowen_mending_circle_1.speaker: Elowen
lines: I set a basket of mismatched socks by the inn's warm stove. There is always one more pair than anyone remembers.
The small repairs are easier when we do them together and talk about something else.

side_elowen_mending_circle_2.speaker: Elowen
lines: We have started a mending circle after the laundry is folded. Juniper reads aloud while everyone works at their own pace.
Nobody checks how much anyone finishes. The company is the point.

side_elowen_mending_circle_3.speaker: Elowen
lines: A traveller left a patch shaped like a little boat on the shared blanket. We kept it there, beside the square one and the wobbly moon.
The blanket is warm now, and it remembers many hands.

side_stellan_lost_property_1.speaker: Stellan
lines: The lost-property cupboard at the station has one drawer that never fills up, however many umbrellas I hand out. I have stopped asking why.
Today it held a ticket stub with no destination, only a name in pencil. I keep it on the shelf where the light is kindest.

side_stellan_lost_property_2.speaker: Stellan
lines: The name on the stub was Osric's, and the morning he asked after, I had a drawer full of mornings nobody collected. The Conductor only touched his cap and nodded at me, as one porter to another.
I think the drawer is a door that goes one way: things the world forgets drift through it. So I label each one carefully. A label is a small promise to come back.

side_stellan_lost_property_3.speaker: Stellan
lines: I pinned a new line to the station timetable in my best handwriting: 'Between: all welcome, no ticket required.' Nobody has complained. A child asked to ring the departure bell for it.
The drawer is nearly empty now. Things are being collected, one name at a time, and I will miss the weight of it, but only a little.

side_iona_undeliverable_post_1.speaker: Iona
lines: My route has a few addresses that make me double-check my bag: the sea, the third star from the lamp post, a Mr. Nobody on Quiet Street. I deliver them all anyway.
A letter that is trying so hard to arrive makes it feel rude to stop. Besides, the sea always accepts its post politely.

side_iona_undeliverable_post_2.speaker: Iona
lines: Mara showed me the old map, and the vanished street on it. I realised my Quiet Street postcards were meant for a house that lives in the gap. I took one there at dusk and the door was waiting, painted blue, just as the postmark remembered.
A name on an envelope is a kind of knock. If enough people knock, a door may remember it is allowed to open.

side_iona_undeliverable_post_3.speaker: Iona
lines: The postcard came back stamped in ink the colour of the harbour at night: 'Received, with thanks. Please keep sending.' Mara has pinned it in the post office window.
So now I carry two bags: one for the places on the map, and a smaller one for the places that are not. I have never loved a route more.

side_liora_lantern_folds_1.speaker: Liora
lines: After each festival, I unfold the old paper lanterns and press them flat under books. Every crease is where somebody's thumb pressed while they made a wish.
Pip stood very still by the window while I worked, as if he knew the folds. I did not ask. Some memories prefer to be handled gently and not questioned.

side_liora_lantern_folds_2.speaker: Liora
lines: When Elias said the lighthouse beam had returned, I found one lantern that had gone warm all by itself in the drawer. Its folds make a harbour, a boat, a keeper's hand holding a lamp.
Memories turn into objects here when nobody is left to carry them. I am only a restorer. My work is to see that they are not carried alone.

side_liora_lantern_folds_3.speaker: Liora
lines: For the beacon's return we made a hundred new lanterns, each with one forgotten name folded into its base. People wrote names they thought were lost, and the paper held them.
We set them afloat on the harbour. They did not drift out to sea. They drifted home, and the lamp was lit by morning.

side_rowan_storeroom_ledger_1.speaker: Rowan
lines: The lighthouse storeroom is tidy, but things leave it quietly. Pencils, mostly. Last week it was a whole box, and I counted twice.
I tell myself the keepers lose them. The tally in my ledger says otherwise: they are going somewhere on purpose.

side_rowan_storeroom_ledger_2.speaker: Rowan
lines: I found a log in the bottom crate, in Elias's handwriting, describing the Long Midnight. He had forgotten writing it, and I almost kept quiet. Then I wondered who the log was waiting for.
I brought it to him with a pot of coffee and sat while he read. Nobody should read their own forgotten words alone.

side_rowan_storeroom_ledger_3.speaker: Rowan
lines: I added a new line to the requisition list: 'Lamp oil, one tin. Pencils, plenty. Welcome, unlimited.' The Conductor sent word that the missing pencils are being used to write names in the ledger on the platform.
So the stores are not lost, only borrowed for kind work. I have decided to stock a few extra, in case the Between runs short.

side_maribel_room_seven_1.speaker: Maribel
lines: The inn has a Room Seven that no traveller has ever booked. I make the bed every morning anyway, and every morning the pillow is faintly warm.
My grandmother said a key left on its hook is a promise to somebody. She never said who.

side_maribel_room_seven_2.speaker: Maribel
lines: A guest signed the register last night in ink that faded before the page dried. I copied the name underneath in pencil, so the book would not forget him.
Names stay put when someone writes them twice. I have started doing that for every sleepy stranger, even the ones who arrive by roads I cannot find on any map.

side_maribel_room_seven_3.speaker: Maribel
lines: Mara thinks the warm pillow was never a ghost. It is the inn remembering a guest who has not found the door yet. Room Seven is simply waiting.
So I left a lamp on the sill and a note on the hook: whoever you are, the kettle is on. Tell Moonmart that if someone wanders in looking for a bed, I will have honey cake ready.

side_tomas_threshold_stone_1.speaker: Tomas
lines: Every stone I set gets a tiny mark on its hidden face and a quiet word before the mortar goes on. Hold well. It is not magic. It is manners.
Still, the old square's wall has never once cracked where I said the word.

side_tomas_threshold_stone_2.speaker: Tomas
lines: Digging the thyme bed, I hit a doorstep. Worn in the middle by years of feet, with no house, no wall, no gate to belong to. Nobody I ask remembers it.
It is warm in the mornings, like a stone someone just stood on. I could not bring myself to break it up for rubble.

side_tomas_threshold_stone_3.speaker: Tomas
lines: I set the doorstep at the end of the square's wall, with a gap left open beside it. A wall that remembers a street should leave room for one.
Lucien says doors remember who they were for. Juniper wrote the stone into her catalogue. I planted thyme beside it, and the first person to pause there stayed a good while.

side_juniper_margin_index_1.speaker: Juniper
lines: I keep an index of the margins. Not the printed stories, the pencilled notes: small kindnesses, jokes, someone's shopping list used as a bookmark.
Pip's cold-milk habit is in there too, now. Memories pile up and become objects if you let them. I just give them a drawer.

side_juniper_margin_index_2.speaker: Juniper
lines: Since the Conductor's visit, I have been finding index cards I do not remember writing. A name at the top, nothing underneath. Every one is in my handwriting.
I keep them in a drawer marked Unclaimed. If a name has weight, it should have somewhere to rest while the world catches up.

side_juniper_margin_index_3.speaker: Juniper
lines: Osric's card is no longer blank. It says: Kept bees. Hums while he works. Back where he belongs. I wrote it and cried a little on the ink.
The forgotten do not vanish, you know. They drift, like lanterns on slow water. The Unclaimed drawer is open for anyone who wants to find a name, or lend one.

side_beckett_morning_thanks_1.speaker: Beckett
lines: My father taught me to thank the water before the first net goes in. I always felt silly saying it aloud, so I whispered.
Sabine heard me from the harbour steps and said thanks carry further than you would think. The nets have come up heavier since, and I try not to ask why.

side_beckett_morning_thanks_2.speaker: Beckett
lines: A glass float came up in my net, warm as a fresh roll. When I held it I smelled my father's pipe and heard him counting gulls.
Fern says seeds can keep a morning inside them too. I set the float by the scales, where the ice cannot reach it.

side_beckett_morning_thanks_3.speaker: Beckett
lines: Elias's beacon brought a little grey boat to the far pier last night. Nobody aboard, and nobody on the harbour remembered her name.
I did. She is my father's Marigold, the boat everyone stopped mentioning after he retired. The glass float fits her lantern hook exactly.
I repainted her name this morning, slowly. Some things come home as soon as someone says them again.

side_nella_seam_names_1.speaker: Nella
lines: Wren asked me to mend her travelling cloak, and my usual thread would not take. It wanted to be told whose cloak it was.
I said her name aloud while I sewed. The stitch held as though it had been waiting.

side_nella_seam_names_2.speaker: Nella
lines: The Conductor's coat has a pocket that opens somewhere else. I sewed a button on it so it only opens when asked politely.
Last night I found a stitch of mine in a seam I never worked. It was older than my hands, and it was mending my mending.

side_nella_seam_names_3.speaker: Nella
lines: It was my grandmother's stitch. She went through a door in the old workroom long ago, and I thought the family had simply forgotten her.
I slipped a crescent handkerchief through the pocket. An hour later a thread came back, knotted around a little bell button.
I wear it on my cuff now. It means someone is pleased with my work, from very far away.

side_aster_starlight_notes_1.speaker: Aster
lines: My notebook lists a star I have not seen yet. The date is next Friday, and the handwriting is mine.
Elias says it is a coincidence. He says it very politely, and looks at the beam while he says it.

side_aster_starlight_notes_2.speaker: Aster
lines: I watched from the lantern gallery while the beacon swept past. For one breath I saw tomorrow's sunrise, thin and gold over the harbour.
Time in the Between does not always move forward, so some light arrives before it leaves. Elias and I agreed not to tell the weather.

side_aster_starlight_notes_3.speaker: Aster
lines: Names have power, so I took care choosing one. The new star is called Marmalade, because it is orange and refuses to be catalogued.
Miso approved by sitting on the chart. I took that as a signature.
I will keep watching so nothing up there is ever forgotten. A star is only lost when everyone stops looking.

lines.speaker: Agnes
lines.text: Lucien, I saved you the little end piece. It has just the right amount of frosting.

lines.speaker: Lucien
lines.text: You remembered my preferred frosting ratio. This is practically a love letter.

lines.speaker: Agnes
lines.text: It's a pastry, dear. Though you may inspect the crumbs for clues.

lines.speaker: Lucien
lines.text: A mystery with crumbs. At last, a genre I understand.

lines.speaker: Agnes
lines.text: You always bring a little green on your sleeves.

lines.speaker: Fern
lines.text: The grove lends its smallest leaves a ride into town.

lines.speaker: Agnes
lines.text: I hope they like the warmth in here.

lines.speaker: Fern
lines.text: They do. The kettle makes a very patient rain.

lines.speaker: Wren
lines.text: Your moonflowers are leaning toward the window.

lines.speaker: Fern
lines.text: They like seeing where their tea goes.

lines.speaker: Fern
lines.text: That too. Plants can be fond of more than one thing.

lines.speaker: Lucien
lines.text: Do people ever return a book with a note tucked inside?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Often. The note is usually the part I read twice.

lines.speaker: Lucien
lines.text: Then I shall look more carefully at the return slot.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Just leave the stamps to me.
